Chapter Seven: The State, Ideology, and the Maintenance of Power.
So, why does capitalism keep going, even when it seems to be in constant crisis? Well, to really get that, we’ve got to look at how the state and ideology play their part.
Now, when you hear “the state,” you might picture some kind of fair referee, just keeping the rules. But in reality, the state is shaped by those with the most power—usually the ruling class. Its laws and institutions aren’t just about order; they’re designed to protect private property, make sure contracts are enforced, and keep things running smoothly—even if that means the majority, the people who actually do the work, get the short end of the stick.
But there’s more to it than just cops and courts. The state also shapes the way we think. That’s what we mean by ideology. Through schools, the media, religion, and everyday culture, those with power spread beliefs that make the current system seem not just normal, but the only way things could be. You’re told that competition is just human nature, that inequality is something we have to accept, and that the market is the best way—maybe the only way—to organize society.
This isn’t always loud or obvious. In fact, it’s usually so subtle you barely notice it. But it’s incredibly effective. It sets the boundaries for what seems possible, or even worth hoping for. Think about how often you hear, “There is no alternative.” That phrase gets repeated so much, it starts to feel like common sense—even if there are plenty of facts that suggest otherwise.
So, let’s break down how power is actually maintained:
The state enforces property rights and doesn’t hesitate to crack down on dissent.
Ideology shapes our beliefs, making it hard to imagine real change.
And then there’s division and distraction—things like racism, nationalism, or just constant consumerism. These are used to weaken solidarity, keeping people from joining together for real change.
But here’s something important: The state and ideology aren’t all-powerful. They’re actually sites of struggle, where different interests and ideas compete for control. Social movements, unions, alternative media—these all have the power to poke holes in the dominant story, and push for something better.
The fact that we see protest and resistance, again and again, is proof that power’s grip is never absolute.
Maybe the best way to picture this is to imagine society as a stage play. Sure, the ruling class writes most of the script and sets the scenery, but the actors—that’s us—can always improvise, resist, or even rewrite the story altogether. The state and ideology are tools for keeping the current order, but they’re also arenas where new possibilities can be born.
